title: Hanuman carries them up
hookLine: the disguise comes off, and Hanuman carries two princes up the mountain
last: TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL SPEECH IS A PRACTICE.

cards: Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are.
Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva.
A wary prince might give a stranger the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.

teach.b: Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that with the whole story, including a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya: Rama, who used to be a refuge for others, has come to Sugriva for refuge.
Hanuman is glad. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom, he says. You can help each other.
Then the disguise comes off. He takes his own shape, a monkey, the son of the Wind.
Rishyamuka is steep and the brothers have walked a long way, so he lifts them onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva.
Here's why that picture matters so much to Hindus. Hanuman is the great example of dasya, devotion as service: loving God by doing God's work, with no wish to be the hero.
Hindu teachers count dasya among the classic ways of devotion, and Hanuman is the one they point to. So Hindus don't pray to Hanuman instead of Rama. They pray to him on the way to Rama.
In many temples his image stands near Rama's, hands joined.
Many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and one line calls him the guardian at Rama's door.
Today's scene is that line in action: the servant who carries tired people to Rama. As for his name, the old bear Jambavan tells that story much later.
As a baby he leapt at the rising sun, thinking it was a fruit, and Indra's thunderbolt struck his jaw, his hanu.

how: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art. In many temples Hanuman's image stands near Rama's with hands joined, and many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

o: the thunderbolt that Indra hurls at his enemies
the jaw, the part of the body behind a well-known name
the wind god said to be the monkey's own father

games.q: the end of the first meeting — tap the pairs.
p: forty verses, often sung on Tuesdays

s: Lakshmana keeps their story secret from the stranger
he tells it all, and says Rama has come seeking refuge.
Hanuman carries both brothers up the mountain
Hindus pray to Hanuman instead of Rama
they pray to him on the way to Rama: the guardian at Rama's door.

games.q: your little cousin asks why Hanuman is always near Rama in the temple, hands joined. by today's story, what fits?
o: he's Rama's devoted servant, and devotees see him as the one who brings people to Rama.
he's in trouble and is apologizing to Rama.
he's only there to guard the temple's money.
games.why: that's dasya, love that serves: he carried the brothers up to Sugriva, and devotees say he carries them to Rama.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, and feel how much they carry on an ordinary day. If you pray, say the chant many Hindu families use, Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, softly on each out-breath, the way Hanuman keeps Rama's name.
If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and bring to mind one person whose load you could help carry this week, without needing to be thanked.

wordCard.voice: Hanu, the jaw struck by Indra's thunderbolt, which gave Hanuman his name.

orig.note: Sanskrit hanumān (hanumat): in Jambavan's story, named for his hanu, the jaw the thunderbolt struck.

carryVoice: Your line: dasya, love that serves. Hanuman carries tired people to Rama and never asks to be the hero. Until tomorrow.
